claims.text: The premelting and melting behavior of initially solid Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed by an interplay between alloy chemical complexity and nanoscale phase-transition behavior.
A disordered solid solution forms during the proposed thermal response.
Formation of the disordered solid solution is followed by the onset of surface-induced melting.
The high surface-to-volume ratio of the nanoparticles enhances formation of a disordered solid solution.
The enhanced formation of a disordered solid solution leads to a reduction in melting point.
Surface-induced melting is the mechanism governing the nanoparticles' melting-point reduction.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles will have a melting point 20% lower than the corresponding bulk alloy.
The nanoparticles will exhibit a wider premelting temperature range than the bulk alloy.
The proposed mechanism applies to particles between 10 and 50 nm over 500–1500 K.
A melting-point reduction of less than 10% relative to bulk would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to increase the premelting temperature range by at least 50 K would falsify the hypothesis.
